text.en: Asha drew a seedling by a window, then noticed the new growth leaning toward the light. Nearby, a touch-me-not leaf folded after contact.

A tropism is a growth response whose direction depends on the stimulus direction. Examples include responses to light, gravity and water. In a nastic movement, the direction of movement depends on the plant part rather than the direction from which the stimulus arrives. A touch-me-not leaf can fold after touch.
Photosynthesis is the process by which plants prepare their food. It needs sunlight, chlorophyll, carbon dioxide and water, and it gives out oxygen. Plants use sugars made in photosynthesis for energy, storage and building materials. Some sugar can be converted to starch.
Transpiration is the loss of water as water vapour from the aerial parts of the plant, mainly through stomata on the leaf. Stomata also exchange gases. Transpiration pulls water up the plant and cools the leaf.

A shoot may bend during growth when light comes from one side. Compare its direction with the direction of the light. Growth toward light is positive phototropism.
An upright shoot with light from above offers a useful comparison. In a second picture, light arrives from one side. The curved new growth shows a change in shoot direction.

board.text: Compare the direction of light and new growth

text.en: A positive tropism moves growth toward a stimulus or in its direction. A negative tropism moves growth away or in the opposite direction. Identify the stimulus before applying the label.
Many ordinary roots grow downward with gravity, while shoots often grow upward against it. This response to gravity is called gravitropism or geotropism.
Roots can respond to differences in moisture. In a textbook diagram, root growth changes toward the wetter region. This is positive hydrotropism.
A climbing tendril can grow around a support after contact. Its growth direction is affected by which side touches the support. That is thigmotropism.
A pollen tube can grow in response to chemical cues in a flower. Chemotropism describes a directional growth response to a chemical stimulus.
Compare the tendril with the touch-me-not leaf. The leaf folds in its characteristic pattern after touch. The direction of folding is set by its structure.

board.text: Tendril growth and leaf folding are different responses

text.en: A flower may open under certain light or temperature conditions. Nastic movement describes the response when its direction is determined by the structure of the flower.

board.text: Light or temperature can trigger nastic movement

text.en: Photosynthesis uses light energy to build sugars. Green leaves often do most of this work. Water and carbon dioxide provide material for the process.

board.text: Water + carbon dioxide → sugars and oxygen using light

text.en: Chlorophyll is a pigment that absorbs some wavelengths of visible light. It is found in chloroplasts in many leaf cells.
Roots supply much of the plant’s water, and xylem can carry it toward the leaves. Carbon dioxide can enter leaves through tiny openings called stomata.

board.text: Water from roots · carbon dioxide from air

text.en: Oxygen is released during photosynthesis. Plant cells also use oxygen during respiration, which releases usable energy from organic molecules.

board.text: Photosynthesis and respiration have different roles

text.en: Respiration in living plant cells continues day and night when the needed materials are available. Photosynthesis depends on suitable light.
Some sugars move in phloem to growing or storage tissues. Others can become starch in a leaf. A plant can use the products in several ways.

board.text: Sugars can be moved, used or stored

text.en: Transpiration describes water vapour leaving parts of the plant above the ground. Much of it leaves through stomata on leaves.
A stoma is an opening between two guard cells. Changing their shape can widen or narrow the opening. That affects water loss and the entry of carbon dioxide.
Water evaporating from leaf surfaces can help pull water through the xylem. Evaporation can also cool the leaf under some conditions.

board.text: Evaporation helps drive upward water movement

text.en: Warm moving air may carry vapour away from a leaf more quickly than still humid air. Water-loss rate also depends on the plant and whether its stomata are open.

board.text: Temperature, wind and humidity can affect water loss

text.en: A plant on dry soil may close many stomata. This slows water loss, while also reducing the path for carbon dioxide to enter.
Compare leaves of the same kind in two pictures. Small droplets on an inner cover can show water vapour condensed there. A cover without leaves is a useful comparison for background moisture.
Use three clues to review a leaf: where light arrives, how gases pass through openings and where water vapour goes. Those clues connect growth, photosynthesis and transpiration.

board.text: Growth response · sugar production · water loss

problem.en: A stem slowly curves toward a window, while a touch-me-not leaf folds after contact. Classify both responses.

text.en: Compare the stem’s growth direction with the light direction.

why.en: Growth toward the window is positive phototropism.

text.en: Check whether the direction of touch sets the direction of leaf folding.

why.en: The leaf folds in its usual pattern, so it is a nastic response.

prompt.en: A friend says Nastic movements depend on the direction of the stimulus. How will you reply?

points.en: Transpiration is loss of water vapour.
